newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope has busy day ahead of hospitalisation.
newsitem.headline: Pope has busy day ahead of hospitalisation.

text.p: Pope John Paul had an active day packed with audiences and appearances at the Vatican on Saturday prior to entering hospital for an operation to remove his appendix.

The 76-year-old Polish Pope is due to enter Rome's Gemelli Polyclinic on Sunday evening after presiding at a beatification ceremony in St Peter's Square and reading a noon prayer -- his last public ceremony before the operation.
On Saturday morning he received bishops from Latin America and the United States in the Vatican and was then driven into St Peter's Square where he addressed some 30,000 people.

The Pope, who has had a spate of health problems recently, appeared in relatively good form as he was driven around the crowd in a open white jeep, his hand stretched out so that hundreds could touch him as the vehicle drove slowly by.
He read his address in a clear and strong voice and did not seem to be fatigued. His left hand trembled, which some doctors say is a sign the Pope may be suffering from Parkinson's disease.
The Vatican has not denied reports that the Pope may be suffering from Parkinson's or a related neurological disorder.

On Saturday night the Pope is due to recite the rosary before another crowd in the Vatican and on Sunday morning will preside at the beatification ceremony, putting 16 people on the road to sainthood.
The surgery is likely to take place on Tuesday after final tests on Monday, Vatican and medical sources said. The Pope is epected to remain in hospital at least until Saturday.
While in the Gemelli, the Pontiff and a handful of close aides will live in a special, heavily guarded suite with its own chapel and kitchen on the 10th floor of the hospital.

The Vatican said last month that periodic inflammation of the appendix was the cause of three bouts of "intestinal fever" which have ailed the leader of the world's 960 million Roman Catholics since Christmas.
A number of doctors in Italy and abroad who are not treating the Pope have expressed scepticism about the Vatican's official version.
Earlier this week, the Vatican denied an Italian news agency report that the Pope may be suffering from a new tumour. The Pope had a colon tumour removed in a 1992 operation.
Professor Giorgio Ribotta, one of the doctors who signed a September 14 statement saying the Pope had an appendix problem, blasted reports of a tumour as "medical fiction -- an Italian sport".
"Those of us who signed that statement believe that this is the diagnosis, although one can always be wrong," he said.
Ribotta said the operation could last about an hour although it could take longer in the Pope's case because parts of his intestine had already been removed in previous operations.
Some was removed in 1981 following an assassination attempt and more was taken out with the tumour in 1992.

Ribotta also said the Pope could be suffering from adhesions, the joining of normally separate tissues which occurs between loops of intestine after abdominal surgery, and can cause obstructions of the alimentary canal and sometimes sharp pain during digestion.
